overview: Inge the Elder was Swedish king remembered for Christian rule and conflicts preserved in later tradition around Uppsala. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: c. 1080 — Rules in Sweden; late 1000s — Christian-pagan conflict in tradition.
He died in 1110, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Inge the Elder was Swedish king remembered for Christian rule and conflicts preserved in later tradition around Uppsala. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: c. 1080 — Rules in Sweden; late 1000s — Christian-pagan conflict in tradition.
He died in 1110, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Inge the Elder was born c. 1050. His family background is usually placed in House of Stenkil, though early Scandinavian genealogy can be uncertain and politically shaped.
Inge the Elder's early life belonged to the medieval Scandinavian world, where kinship, sea routes, church contacts, assemblies, and armed followings shaped the opportunities available to a ruler.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Inge the Elder is remembered as a firmly Christian Swedish king whose faith brought him into direct conflict with the pagan party, and the saga tradition preserves a vivid story to illustrate it. According to that account, Inge refused to perform the old sacrifices at Uppsala and was driven from the throne for it, replaced by his pagan brother-in-law "Blot-Sven," before returning to kill the usurper and reclaim his kingdom for Christianity.

This narrative, though shaped by later Christian storytelling, presents Inge as devout and resolute, willing to lose his crown rather than compromise his faith and determined enough to win it back. The tradition consistently casts him as a champion of the new religion against the last strength of paganism.

Because the dramatic episodes come from saga sources written long after, they must be read as Christian memory rather than documented fact. But the steady direction of the tradition — a pious, stubborn king who broke with the old cult — gives Inge a clearer reputation than most early Swedish rulers, even if the details belong to legend.

contentSections.title: As king of Sweden
paragraphs: Inge the Elder ruled in a period when Christian monarchy was still contested. Later tradition connects him with conflict over pagan sacrifice at Uppsala, though details are difficult to verify.
As King of Sweden, Inge the Elder had to turn dynastic claim into workable authority through alliances, military pressure, church support, and acceptance by regional elites.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Died around 1105-1110 after helping strengthen Christian royal legitimacy in Sweden; the exact place and circumstances are uncertain.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: He is remembered as a Christianizing king, but much of the narrative depends on later sources.
Later saga, saintly, or national traditions often amplified Inge the Elder's reputation, so the article separates near-contemporary evidence from later memory where possible.

predecessor.note: His brother and co-king, a son of Stenkil; the succession after Stenkil was contested between rival claimants (including two kings named Eric) before the sons of Stenkil ruled.

successor.note: His nephew, who ruled jointly with Inge the Younger as the Stenkil dynasty waned.
